hints: Focus on what links gas volume to moles under room conditions, then moles to molar mass.
Work out the Mr of carbon monoxide, ethene and nitrogen and see which ones match 28 g mol-1.
walkthrough:
**Find moles from gas volume**

Great start, let's turn volume into moles. Under room conditions (r.t.p.), 1 mol of any gas occupies 24.0 dm3, which is 24000 cm3.

$$n = \frac{V}{24.0} = \frac{0.600 \text{ dm}^3}{24.0 \text{ dm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}} = 0.0250 \text{ mol}$$

**Find the molar mass of X**

Now use mass to find Mr. Molar mass is just mass per mole.

$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.700 \text{ g}}{0.0250 \text{ mol}} = 28.0 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$

**Check the three gases**

Let's calculate each Mr and compare to 28.

$$M_r(\text{CO}) = 12.0 + 16.0 = 28.0$$
$$M_r(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4) = (2 \times 12.0) + (4 \times 1.0) = 28.0$$
$$M_r(\text{N}_2) = 2 \times 14.0 = 28.0$$

**Conclude**

All three gases have the same molar mass of 28 g mol-1, so all three could be X. That means statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct. All three gases have Mr = 28, which exactly matches the experimental Mr of 28.0 g mol-1 from 0.700 g in 600 cm3. So 1, 2 and 3 are all possible.
options.B: Incorrect. This would mean only 1 and 2 are correct. Nitrogen also has Mr = 28 ($\text{N}_2$ = 28.0), so there is no reason to exclude statement 3.
options.C: Incorrect. This would mean only 2 and 3 are correct. Carbon monoxide also has Mr = 28 ($\text{CO}$ = 12 + 16 = 28), so statement 1 cannot be left out.
options.D: Incorrect. This would mean only 1 is correct. Ethene ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ = 28) and nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$ = 28) have the same Mr, so they fit the data just as well. This is the classic trap of stopping after one match.
